thesis: This episode argues that the primary driver of value for companies like Disney, Richemont, and Costco is their ability to control distribution and limit supply to protect brand equity, rather than relying solely on product innovation. The speaker also emphasizes the importance of management teams that understand the imperative of 'no' and avoid compensation structures that incentivize cutting brand investment to drive short-term cash flow.

claims.claim: The speaker believes controlling distribution is the exclusive reason for Disney's value, citing their blockbusters and invaluable library.
claims.quote: We think the economics of controlling your distribution will be huge. Look at the limited number of movies that Disney comes out with each year, but they're all blockbusters. These people are very, very good, and they get it. But it's to the theme of controlling distribution. That's really the exclusive reason.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Netflix may be a long-term viable competitor but is unsure if they can replicate Disney's success once they lose content.
claims.quote: I think Netflix may be a long-term viable competitor, but I don't know. So you talk to kids and folks in their 20s. I'm not sure that once they've lost all this content, they can do what Disney has done.

claims.claim: The speaker views Cummins as a cyclical environmental upgrade story with extraordinary R&D, though concerned about battery technology replacing diesel.
claims.quote: So Cummins makes diesel engines. They make diesel engines from Class 8 down to Class 2. So they're bread and butter selling into Picard and Navistar, the big truck manufacturers. So the truck manufacturers always rely on dual source. So they all have their own engine manufacturing in-house, but they don't want to do themselves.

claims.claim: The speaker fears battery technology will replace diesel but believes the weight and charging limitations make it a threat only in the distant future for Class 8 trucks.
claims.quote: So along comes Tesla and Nikola and battery technology. So there's a fear that battery will replace the diesel technology completely. You've got some cities in Europe that are looking to ban diesel engines entirely. We think at a minimum, the Class 8 truck market, which is the big tractor trailers that run over the road. We just don't see that as a threat any time soon.

claims.claim: The speaker admits to owning Microsoft over the years, noting its ability to compound, price, and grow volume despite classical valuation techniques not getting growth right.
claims.quote: We've owned things like Microsoft over the years, though. I mean, having written about Microsoft in early 2000, predicting that shareholders would lose money for 15 years, well, that was exclusively an assessment based on price. Microsoft had had compounded at 65 percent a year, the stock since its 1985 IPO, top line had grown at 50%.

claims.claim: The speaker liked the management, unit economics, and the plan to double store count, noting they are similar to a company they bought.
claims.quote: And very similar to a Costco though, we liked what management was doing. We love the unit economics and management had a plan to basically double the store count over the next, call it 10 to 12 years.

claims.claim: The speaker differentiates it from competitors by its focus on rural markets, noting that shipping small baskets is not economically viable.
claims.quote: 70% of dollar general's business is done in rural markets, which I think differentiates it from their primary dollar store competitors. I think if you're in Amazon and you're trying to ship a basket of $13 worth of goods to Knob Nostra, Nostra, Missouri, it costs you a hell of a lot more than $13 or $14 $14 to ship.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Amazon Prime memberships are increasing in rural areas but believes they will eventually focus on larger basket sizes.
claims.quote: We have seen the increase in Amazon prime memberships, even in rural, go up and up, But they're going to figure out. They already know they don't make money shipping a small basket of goods.

claims.claim: The speaker praises the high gross margins, the chairman's long-term brand focus, and the strategy to control distribution to prevent brand cheapening.
claims.quote: And what I learned quickly was it's far from that. I mean, here's a manufacturer that does 65% gross margins. You're not going to find a lot of manufacturers that run 65% gross margins. And as you run up the curve to more and more valuable or higher price point watches as an example, the gross margins can run into the 90%.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights the strategy to limit supply and control distribution to protect the brand value, even at the expense of operating margins.
claims.quote: So they physically took inventory, bought it back out of the channel from their third-party retail partners and made, in the case of Cartier, a public display out of melting down portions of the watches. They would take the movement out, but they would melt down the precious metal content.

claims.claim: The speaker was attracted to Disney's strategy of controlling distribution by going over the top with their own platforms like Hulu and ESPN.
claims.quote: Well, what did it for us really was when Disney took their property back from Netflix and said, we're going to go over the top and distribute ourselves. Across the business of Disney with the theme park business, with the retail, with the studio business, with the movies.

claims.claim: The speaker believes controlling distribution is the exclusive reason for the investment, noting the stock was cheap due to the arbitrage community driving up Fox.
claims.quote: We just looked at it and said, We think the economics of controlling your distribution will be huge. Look at the limited number of movies that Disney comes out with each year, but they're all blockbusters. These people are very, very good, and they get it.

claims.claim: The speaker describes selling Ross Stores at 10 times earnings as a mistake because the stock became a 20-bagger, indicating it was worth far more than the price paid.
claims.quote: We buy Ross stores, as an example. At maybe 10 times earnings, we'd followed Ross for seven or eight years, had never owned it. Terrific retailer.

claims.claim: The speaker states that after selling Ross Stores, the stock became a 20-bagger, proving it was worth way more than 10 or 20 times earnings.
claims.quote: In the years having sold it since, the stock's more than a 20-bagger, just insane. So you look at the unit count, profitability grew, gross margins expanded.

claims.claim: The speaker admits Ross was worth way more than 10 times earnings and even more than 20 times earnings, making the sale a painful lesson.
claims.quote: Well, it was clearly worth way more than 10. It was worth way more than 20 times. And so that was just a very painfully expensive lesson because it had grown grown into a good size position.

claims.claim: The speaker criticizes General Mills' compensation structure, noting the hurdle for bonus comp declined to a negative 1.4% organic growth rate, meaning they pay to shrink the business.
claims.quote: Well, the number today, the hurdle today is a negative 1.4% organic growth rate. And that's stunning. We're going to pay you performance comp to slowly shrink the business.

claims.claim: The speaker points out that General Mills pays executives on free cash flow and organic sales growth over a rolling three-year period, creating pressure to maintain performance.
claims.quote: The other overlay to the current comp, and this has evolved in the case of General Mills as well, is we're going to pay you on free cash on a rolling three-year period.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Berkshire as a holding company with a collection of business infrastructure that has adeptly pivoted throughout its 55-year history to take advantage of major inflection points in capital markets.
claims.quote: Well, obviously it's a holding company, but unlike any other throughout time, you've got a collection of business infrastructure that I think has very adeptly. pivoted at times throughout the 55-year history that Mr. Buffett has run the business, at times to opportunistically take advantage of major, major inflection points in the capital markets.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Berkshire has morphed from being almost entirely insurance and reinsurance in 1998 to a business where 45% of the overall value is still tethered to property casualty insurance and reinsurance.
claims.quote: So now it's really morphed from what was. I mean, it was almost entirely insurance and reinsurance in 98. They obviously picked up all of Geico along the way. Now you've got a business that probably 45% of the overall value is still tethered to property casualty insurance and reinsurance.

claims.claim: The speaker argues that the Gen Re deal was a great transaction that allowed Berkshire to buy other things like the utility in 2000 and the railroad in 2009 using surplus capital.
claims.quote: And it's the upstreaming of that capital and also the surplus capital that already existed inside of Berkshire that was then more wholly invested in bonds and cash that allowed them to buy the utility in 2000, that allowed them to buy the railroad 2009.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Berkshire's book value is $350 billion today, which is significantly higher than the $110 billion it would have compounded to if the Gen Re deal hadn't occurred.
claims.quote: Well, Berkshire's book value is $350 billion today. So the $80 billion that they've given up in terms of today's pro rata share of Berkshire is the wrong way to look at it. It's what they did with the capital.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Berkshire Hathaway is a vastly more valuable business today than when it was bought, citing masterful capital allocation and a collection of durable assets like railroads and utilities.
claims.quote: Well, Berkshire's book value is $350 billion today. So the $80 billion that they've given up in terms of today's pro rata share of Berkshire is the wrong way to look at it.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the railroad business, once thought to be a crappy business, is now worth about $100 billion, having been bought for $34 billion.
claims.quote: And so on a deal that we thought was outrageous at $34 billion, you know, we think that business today is worth about $100 billion.

claims.claim: The speaker describes the collection of electric utilities owned by Berkshire as arguably the best set of utilities in the business, with good management and tax advantaged returns.
claims.quote: But you think about the collection of electric utilities that they own, they are arguably the best set of utilities in the business. They're in places within the country with higher population growth.

claims.claim: The speaker expresses confidence in Berkshire's management team and succession planning, noting that they have thought long and hard about succession within each operating subsidiary.
claims.quote: And I'm satisfied with what I've seen and all kind of the digging that we've done, that they really have thought long and hard within each of those myriad operating subs about succession planning.

claims.claim: The speaker believes that Berkshire Hathaway has durability and permanence, citing the railroad business as an oligopoly that is hard to displace.
claims.quote: I think the railroad, it is what it is. It exists within an oligopoly. Rational or not, I think more rational here in the last decade. But it's kind of hard to scrub a railroad.

claims.claim: The speaker uses Costco as an example where high CapEx spending masks underlying economic profitability, making free cash flow a misnomer.
claims.quote: You take back to my Costco example, when you have a growing business that can reinvest retained earnings at high incremental returns, the CAPX that's being spent masks underlying economic profitability.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions General Dynamics as an example of a business that has had tailwinds in its underlying industries despite having large defined benefit plans.
claims.quote: Some of these have been still good investments because they've had tailwinds in terms of their underlying industries. But you get the one-off, call it $2 billion one-off.

claims.claim: The speaker uses Ford as an example of a company with a large defined benefit plan relative to the business itself.
claims.quote: And so what happens with those plans is take a Ford. I mean, take any of those. Take a general dynamics. Some of these have been still good investments because they've had tailwinds in terms of their underlying industries.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Berkshire Hathaway has been successful owning well-run property casualty insurers and reinsurers.
claims.quote: But we've had so much success owning well run, property casualty insurers and reinsurers. And the reason I think they work is, as long as we're allowed to do the investing and I don't have to just own the sector, I'm good because I think there are some outstanding insurance people.
